ann_28.text: Through this part, being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 33% to about 4%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 7%, and a reversible thallium defect to about 14% (on the training data only).
Being a woman clearly lowers the predicted risk more if exercise does not bring on chest pain (from about 33% to about 2%, against about 19% to about 9% with it).
Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL clearly lowers it more if exercise does not bring on chest pain (from about 33% to about 8%, against about 19% to about 21% with it).
A reversible thallium defect clearly raises it more if exercise brings on chest pain (from about 19% to about 43%, against about 33% to about 34% without it).
Atypical angina clearly lowers it more if exercise brings on chest pain (from about 19% to about 5%, against about 33% to about 11% without it).
On its own through this part, atypical angina changes the predicted risk only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_29.text: This part barely changes the predictions.
Through it, an ST segment that does not slope up at peak exercise raises a typical patient's predicted risk only slightly, from about 33% to about 35% (on the training data only).

ann_30.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 4%), non-anginal chest pain (about 7%) or atypical angina (about 11%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 33%).

More vessels coloured raise the predicted risk steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: a typical patient goes from about 33% at 0 vessels to about 94% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher (on the training data only).
A flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 81% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise (about 25% at 0 mm to about 61% at 2.8 mm), higher cholesterol (about 21% at 193 mg/dL to about 56% at 308 mg/dL) and older age (about 22% at 42 years to about 43% at 66 years) raise the predicted risk steadily (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it from about 33% to about 2% (on the training data only).

The model has little data on three categories: a thallium result coded 4 (2 patients; about 94%), a fixed defect on the thallium scan (15 patients; about 22%) and a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 42%), all on the training data only.
A reversible defect on the thallium scan raises it only slightly overall, to about 34% (on the training data only).
It ignores the resting ECG, the maximum heart rate and resting blood pressure.

ann_28.original: Hypothesis: a sex x exercise-angina interaction built from two chained ReLU gates. Gate 1213 = relu(1.23 sex:0 + 1.31 exang:0 - 0.509 cp:2 - 0.563 fbs:0 + 0.476 thal:7 + 0.091) is a female-without-exercise-angina score; gate 47 = relu(1.43 + 0.956 exang:0 - 1.93 h1213) fires for patients without exercise angina whose 1213 score is low (mostly men) and is shut off by 1213. The output reads -0.760 h1213 + 0.384 g47. Evidence (train, n=242): group mean block logit is +0.04 (male, exang), +0.18 (male, no exang), -0.39 (female, exang), -1.76 (female, no exang). Exercise angina has no direct edge to the output, so its entire effect is this block: flipping exang no->yes raises the logit by +1.81 on average for women (range 0.78..2.11) but by -0.17 for men (range -0.78..1.87). g47 is active for 84% of men without angina but 19% of women without angina. cp:2, fbs:0 and thal:7 only shift h1213 (sensitivities 0.22-0.26 vs 0.57-0.60 for sex:0/exang:0). Odd signs (thal:7 and fbs:1 making the block slightly less protective / more protective respectively) are small modifiers we do not interpret clinically. Ablating gate 47 to its mean drops train AUC 0.9457->0.9414; ablating 1213->output drops it to 0.9347.
ann_28.proposed: Through this part, whether exercise brings on chest pain changes how other factors act: without it, being a woman and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lower the predicted risk more; with it, a reversible thallium defect raises the risk more and atypical angina lowers it more.

ann_29.original: Hypothesis: a near-inert affine pass-through of slope:1 (upsloping ST segment). Evidence: the ReLU pre-activation 0.446 slope:1 + 0.797 lies in [0.373, 1.266] on train, so it never clips; through the -0.0648 readout it adds -0.029 slope:1 - 0.052 to the logit (logit SD 0.029). Ablating it to its mean changes train AUC 0.9457->0.9454. It is a vestigial linear term, slightly protective for upsloping ST.
ann_29.proposed: A part that barely changes the predictions; an ST segment that does not slope up raises the risk only slightly through it.

ann_30.original: Hypothesis: the risk logit is additive: a logistic-regression core over 14 direct input edges (dominated by ca +1.57, cp:4 +1.30, slope:2 +1.04, oldpeak +0.66, chol +0.65, thal:7 +0.58; all risk-raising except thal:6 -0.13) plus two child terms: -0.760 h1213 + 0.384 g47 from sex_exang_interaction (the only route by which exercise angina affects risk, and only materially for women) and -0.065 x 3660 from slope1_offset (near-inert). The output node applies ReLU and the model then applies a sigmoid, so p = sigmoid(relu(z)): negative logits (60% of train) all map to p=0.5 and the decision is z>0. The 8 inputs cp:1, trestbps, restecg:0/1/2, thalach, exang:1 and thal:3 have no edges in the phenotype and are included as entries with zero effect. Evidence (train, n=242): full AUC 0.9457 / acc 0.876; linear core alone (children at their means) AUC 0.9255 / acc 0.855; logit SD 3.58 total, 3.42 linear core, 1.04 interaction block, 0.029 slope:1 term. Node-0 sensitivity ranks ca 0.63, cp:4 0.52, slope:2 0.42, oldpeak 0.27, chol 0.26, exang:0 0.26 (via the block).
ann_30.proposed: Typical angina, non-anginal chest pain and atypical angina lower the predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms. More vessels coloured, a flat ST segment, more ST depression, higher cholesterol and older age raise it; being a woman lowers it. The model ignores the resting ECG, the maximum heart rate and resting blood pressure.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk about 33%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 4%), non-anginal chest pain (about 7%) or atypical angina (about 11%).

More vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raise the predicted risk steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: for a typical patient it goes from about 33% at 0 vessels to about 94% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

Being a woman lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient it clearly falls from about 33% to about 2% without chest pain on exercise, and from about 19% to about 9% with it.

A reversible defect on the thallium scan raises the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise brings on chest pain: it clearly moves from about 19% to about 43% with chest pain on exercise, and from about 33% to about 34% without it.

Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL clearly lowers the predicted risk if exercise does not bring on chest pain (from about 33% to about 8%), while with chest pain on exercise it moves from about 19% to about 21%.
It ignores the resting ECG, the maximum heart rate and resting blood pressure.

worth_checking.text: Worth checking: the model treats fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL as lowering the risk of heart disease for patients without chest pain on exercise (for a typical patient from about 33% to about 8%).

Worth checking: the model treats a fixed defect on the thallium scan as lowering the risk compared with a normal scan, from only 15 training patients.

worth_checking.text: Worth checking: the model gives a very high predicted risk to the 2 training patients whose thallium result is coded 4, a code the dataset documentation does not define.
Worth checking: the model ignores resting blood pressure.
Worth checking: the model ignores the maximum heart rate reached during the exercise test.
Worth checking: the model ignores the resting ECG.

worth_checking.flag: reversible thallium defect lowers risk through one part
worth_checking.text: Worth checking: through one part, a reversible thallium defect lowers the predicted risk of a typical patient, although overall it raises it slightly.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

values.fbs: fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_28.text: The model gives a clearly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect than if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan, and even more so if exercise brings on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from thallium stress test result other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan to a reversible defect on the thallium scan moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 19% to about 43% if exercise brings on chest pain, and from about 33% to about 34% if exercise does not bring on chest pain.

The model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL than if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less to fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 33% to about 8% if exercise does not bring on chest pain, and from about 19% to about 21% if exercise brings on chest pain.

The model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman than if the patient is a man, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from male to female moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 33% to about 2% if exercise does not bring on chest pain, and from about 19% to about 9% if exercise brings on chest pain.

For a typical patient, going from chest pain type other than atypical angina to atypical angina moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 19% to about 5% if exercise brings on chest pain, and from about 33% to about 11% if exercise does not bring on chest pain.

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman (about 4%) than if the patient is a man (about 33%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL (about 7%) than if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less (about 33%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect (about 14%) than if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan (about 33%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has atypical angina (about 33%) than if chest pain type is something other than atypical angina (about 33%) (on the training data only).

ann_29.text: Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than an upsloping ST segment (about 35%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 33%) (on the training data only).
This part barely changes the model's predictions (by at most 0.8 percentage points).

ann_30.text: The model treats a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: for a typical patient, it goes from about 33% at 0 vessels to about 94% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded) applies (about 94%) than if the thallium scan is normal (about 33%) (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 2 training patients (thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded)).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 81%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 33%) (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher ST depression on exercise as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 25% at 0.0 mm to about 61% at 2.8 mm (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher serum cholesterol as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 21% at 193 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L) to about 56% at 308 mg/dL (8.0 mmol/L) (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman (about 2%) than if the patient is a man (about 33%) (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has typical angina (about 4%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 33%).
For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has non-anginal chest pain (about 7%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 33%).
For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has atypical angina (about 11%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 33%).
The model treats a higher age as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 22% at 42 years to about 43% at 66 years (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the thallium scan shows a fixed defect (about 22%) than if the thallium scan is normal (about 33%) (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment slopes down at peak exercise (about 42%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 33%) (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).

For a typical patient, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect (about 34%) than if the thallium scan is normal (about 33%) (on the training data only).
It ignores resting ECG, maximum heart rate reached during the exercise test and resting blood pressure.
